name: project_bridge_tailscale_launch
description: cmux-bridge Tailscale/launch gotcha — a stale orphaned process holding :47821 makes the rebuilt binary die on LAN bind before tsnet starts
metadata:

---

The bridge binds LAN (`net.Listen(":47821")`) **before** starting the Tailscale
`tsnet` listener, and treats a LAN bind failure as `log.Fatalf`. So if a previous
`cmux-bridge` process still holds :47821, every restart dies with
`lan listen :47821: bind: address already in use` **before tsnet ever runs** —
Tailscale silently never comes up and the phone only works on Wi‑Fi.

`launchctl unload` / `kickstart -k` do NOT kill an instance that has reparented to
launchd (PPID 1) — that's exactly how the stale holder survives. Diagnosed 2026-07-16:
one orphan (old pre-tailscale binary, started before the 23:56 rebuild) held the port
while launchd crash-looped the new binary every 10s. Zero `tailscale:` lines in a 33k-line
log = tsnet code path never reached. Fix was `kill <pid>`; launchd respawned the new
binary which then logged `tailscale: listening on cmux-bridge.tail901772.ts.net:47821`.

Fixed in `scripts/install-bridge.sh` (2026-07-16): it now `pkill -f`s all instances,
waits for :47821 to free, then loads + verifies both `ws: listening` and (with
`--tailscale`) `tailscale: listening on` in the log tail. Also added a no-sudo guard
(per-user LaunchAgent) and sudo-only-for-binary-copy.

Tailnet host is embedded in the pairing QR at `--pair` time (via tsnet DNS name). If
the phone was paired without `--tailscale`, its credentials have no `.ts.net` host and
iOS never falls back off-LAN — **must re-pair with `cmux-bridge --pair --tailscale`**.
The daemon and `--pair` share the tsnet state dir (`~/.config/cmux-bridge/tailscale`),
so stop the daemon before pairing if the state is locked.

Debug: `grep -E "ws: listening|tailscale: listening" ~/Library/Logs/cmux-bridge.log`;
`lsof -nP -iTCP:47821 -sTCP:LISTEN`; `curl -m4 -o/dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:47821/ws` → 401 means healthy (Bearer required). Related: [[reference_ios_build_cmd]].

content.text:
Confirmed. There are two pieces:

**1. Install/run the daemon with Tailscale enabled:**
```
scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale
```

**2. Pair your phone so the credentials embed the `.ts.net` host (required for off-LAN access):**
```
cmux-bridge --pair --tailscale
```

Key gotchas from past setup:
- **You must pair *with* `--tailscale`.** If the phone was paired without it, its credentials have no `.ts.net` host and iOS won't fall back off Wi-Fi — you have to re-pair.
- The daemon and `--pair` share the tsnet state dir (`~/.config/cmux-bridge/tailscale`), so **stop the daemon before pairing** if the state is locked.
- If a restart fails, a stale `cmux-bridge` process may be holding `:47821`, which kills the rebuild before tsnet starts. Check with `lsof -nP -iTCP:47821 -sTCP:LISTEN` and `kill <pid>` (launchctl won't kill a launchd-reparented orphan).

Verify it's up:
```
grep -E "ws: listening|tailscale: listening" ~/Library/Logs/cmux-bridge.log
```

# cmux-companion

iPhone companion app for [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) — mirror notifications, control workspaces, navigate surfaces, and send voice commands from your phone.

## Architecture

```
[cmux Mac app]  <── Unix socket ──>  [cmux-bridge]  <── WebSocket/LAN ──>  [iOS app]
```

- **`bridge/`** — Go binary that connects to the local cmux socket and exposes a WebSocket server on the LAN
- **`ios/`** — SwiftUI iPhone app (landscape, iOS 17+)
- **`shared/`** — Protocol documentation

## Prerequisites

- [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) with socket control enabled:
  **Settings > Socket Control > Password mode**
- Go 1.21+ (to build the bridge)
- Xcode 15+ (to build the iOS app)
- macOS 13+
- iOS 17+
- Mac and iPhone on the same local network

## Setup

### 1. Build the bridge

```bash
cd bridge
go build -o cmux-bridge ./cmd/cmux-bridge
sudo mv cmux-bridge /usr/local/bin/
```

Or use the install script (builds + sets up LaunchAgent for auto-start on login).
Run it **as your normal user, not with `sudo`** — it installs a per-user
LaunchAgent, and it will ask for sudo only if `/usr/local/bin` needs it:

```bash
./scripts/install-bridge.sh            # LAN only
./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale  # LAN + remote access (recommended)
```

The script hard-kills any previous bridge process and waits for the port to free
before starting the freshly-built binary, then verifies it's listening (and, with
`--tailscale`, that the tailnet listener came up). This avoids a stale daemon
silently keeping the old binary alive — see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### 2. First-time pairing

This only needs to be done once. It connects to cmux's socket, generates a token, and shows a QR code.

```bash
cmux-bridge --pair
```

You'll be prompted for the cmux socket password (if password mode is enabled in cmux Settings > Socket Control). Then a QR code appears in the terminal — keep it visible for the next step.

### 3. Build and run the iOS app

iPhone companion app for [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) — mirror notifications, control workspaces, navigate surfaces, and send voice commands from your phone.

## Architecture

```
[cmux Mac app]  <── Unix socket ──>  [cmux-bridge]  <── WebSocket/LAN ──>  [iOS app]
```

- **`bridge/`** — Go binary that connects to the local cmux socket and exposes a WebSocket server on the LAN
- **`ios/`** — SwiftUI iPhone app (landscape, iOS 17+)
- **`shared/`** — Protocol documentation

## Prerequisites

- [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) with socket control enabled:
  **Settings > Socket Control > Password mode**
- Go 1.21+ (to build the bridge)
- Xcode 15+ (to build the iOS app)
- macOS 13+
- iOS 17+
- Mac and iPhone on the same local network

## Setup

### 1. Build the bridge

```bash
cd bridge
go build -o cmux-bridge ./cmd/cmux-bridge
sudo mv cmux-bridge /usr/local/bin/
```

Or use the install script (builds + sets up LaunchAgent for auto-start on login).
Run it **as your normal user, not with `sudo`** — it installs a per-user
LaunchAgent, and it will ask for sudo only if `/usr/local/bin` needs it:

```bash
./scripts/install-bridge.sh            # LAN only
./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale  # LAN + remote access (recommended)
```

The script hard-kills any previous bridge process and waits for the port to free
before starting the freshly-built binary, then verifies it's listening (and, with
`--tailscale`, that the tailnet listener came up). This avoids a stale daemon
silently keeping the old binary alive — see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### 2. First-time pairing

This only needs to be done once. It connects to cmux's socket, generates a token, and shows a QR code.

```bash
cmux-bridge --pair
```

You'll be prompted for the cmux socket password (if password mode is enabled in cmux Settings > Socket Control). Then a QR code appears in the terminal — keep it visible for the next step.

### 3. Build and run the iOS app

No `make` command — there's no Makefile. Setup is documented in the README and driven by two shell scripts in `scripts/`:

- **`scripts/build.sh`** — builds the bridge binary
- **`scripts/install-bridge.sh [--tailscale]`** — builds + installs the LaunchAgent (auto-start on login), kills stale instances, and verifies the listener came up

The README's first-clone flow is:

1. **Build + install the bridge daemon:**
   ```bash
   ./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale   # or without flag for LAN only
   ```
   (Run as your normal user, *not* sudo — it's a per-user LaunchAgent.)

2. **Pair once:**
   ```bash
   cmux-bridge --pair --tailscale
   ```

3. **Build + run the iOS app** in Xcode.

There's no single `make setup` that does all three (the iOS build is inherently an Xcode step). If you want, I can add a `Makefile` (or a `scripts/setup.sh`) that wraps steps 1–2 into one `make setup` target — the iOS app would still need Xcode. Want me to?

Found the root cause. That `/tmp/cmux.sock` path is the bridge's **last-resort fallback** — it's only used when the bridge can't find cmux's real socket anywhere. So on your mac mini, cmux never created its control socket.

```
~/Library/Application Support/cmux/last-socket-path
```

The bridge's detection order is: `last-socket-path` file → `~/.local/state/cmux/cmux-<uid>.sock` → `~/Library/Application Support/cmux/cmux.sock` → then finally `/tmp/cmux.sock`. Getting `/tmp/cmux.sock` means **all** the real paths came up empty on the mini.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)

- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |

## Problem

Setting up the bridge on a fresh Mac (a Mac mini) failed with:

```
cannot connect to cmux socket: connect /tmp/cmux.sock: dial unix /tmp/cmux.sock: connect: no such file or directory
```

`/tmp/cmux.sock` is `DetectSocketPath`'s last-resort fallback, so hitting it means **every** real candidate missed even though cmux was running with a live socket.

## Root cause

On the mini, cmux wrote:
- the pointer file at `~/.local/state/cmux/last-socket-path` (XDG state dir), **not** under Application Support, and
- the socket as `~/.local/state/cmux/cmux.sock` — the plain name, **not** `cmux-<uid>.sock`.

1. only read the `last-socket-path` pointer from `~/Library/Application Support/cmux/` (missed the XDG one), and
2. its direct-socket fallback hardcoded `cmux-<uid>.sock` (missed the plain `cmux.sock`).

So all candidates failed and it fell through to `/tmp/cmux.sock`.

## Fix

Probe all known locations before the `/tmp` fallback:
- read the `last-socket-path` pointer from **both** the XDG state dir and Application Support, preferring one whose socket actually exists (with the first non-empty pointer kept as a fallback);
- probe both the uid-suffixed (`cmux-<uid>.sock`) and plain (`cmux.sock`) socket names in each directory.

EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -5

`socket_path` in `~/.config/cmux-bridge/config.json`, which short-circuits detection

defaults). Used this on the mini pointing at `/Users/m/.local/state/cmux/cmux.sock`.

Perfect. Now I have all the information I need. Let me create a comprehensive report.

## Investigation Results

### **Direction 1: Multiple iOS clients on one bridge**

**Verdict: YES - Multiple concurrent WebSocket connections are supported.**

The bridge WebSocket server **does accept multiple concurrent connections** and broadcasts events to all clients:

**Evidence:**

1. **Multiple concurrent connections accepted**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/bridge/internal/ws/server.go:66-90`
   - The `Server.Serve()` method accepts multiple `net.Listener` instances and can serve from multiple listeners simultaneously (LAN + Tailscale)
   - Each `handleClient()` call (line 52) processes one independent WebSocket connection
   - The HTTP handler creates a fresh `conn` per request with no per-server singleton connection variable

2. **Stateless per-connection handler**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/bridge/internal/ws/handler.go:40-129`
   - `handleClient()` takes `w, r` (request/response) and manages one connection in isolation
   - No single-client enforcement; multiple simultaneous calls are safe
   - Each connection gets its own `events` channel subscription (line 79) and `incoming` channel (line 83)

3. **Broadcast to all subscribers**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/bridge/internal/poller/poller.go:77-92`
   - `Poller.Broadcast()` sends events to **all** subscribers in `p.subscribers[]` (a slice, line 37)
   - Line 85: iterates over all subscribers and sends without assuming a single client
   - Line 131-139: notification events loop through all subs and send to each

4. **Reusable, non-single-use token**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/bridge/internal/pair/qr.go:18-41` and `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/bridge/internal/ws/auth.go:9-23`
   - The token is generated once and persisted to disk: `LoadOrCreateToken()` (line 18)
   - Used across daemon restarts and multiple connections
   - Auth check is simple Bearer token validation (line 22) — no per-connection token consumption or revocation
   - Same token can authenticate unlimited concurrent WebSocket connections

**Limitation**: Fast consumers with small event buffers (line 56 in handler.go: `make(chan Event, 32)`) may drop events if overloaded, but connections won't fail; they'll silently miss notifications.

---

### **Direction 2: One iOS app managing multiple bridges/Macs**

**Verdict: NO - Only one bridge can be paired at a time.**

The iOS app stores a **single** bridge (one host/port/token tuple) and can only connect to one server:

**Evidence:**

1. **Single-entry Keychain storage**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/ios/cmux/Connection/PairingStore.swift:18-73`
   - `PairingStore` uses a single hardcoded Keychain entry: `service = "dev.itsmaleen.cmux-bridge"` + `account = "credentials"` (lines 19-20)
   - `save()` (line 22): Deletes any existing entry before adding new one (line 31), so only one credential set is kept
   - `load()` (line 46): Fetches a single `PairingCredentials` (line 59); returns one struct, not a list

2. **Single paired bridge in AppState**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:31-32`
   - `private let pairingStore = PairingStore()` — one store instance
   - `private var client: BridgeClient?` — one client (line 32), not a list/dictionary
   - `@Published var pendingPairing: PairingCredentials?` (line 68) — single pending pairing, not a queue

3. **Overwrite on re-pair**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:85-89`
   - `handlePairingURL()` checks if the new pairing is different from the existing one
   - If different, only `pendingPairing` is set; if same or first-time, it overwrites via `commitPairing()`
   - No UI option to add/keep multiple bridges; line 94-99 saves one credential and disconnects the old client

4. **Settings view shows single bridge**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/ios/cmux/Settings/SettingsView.swift:7-45`
   - `credentials` is `PairingCredentials?` (line 7), not an array
   - Only one host/port/tailscale pair displayed
   - "Pair new device" (line 62) triggers re-pairing flow, not adding a second bridge

5. **Single active connection**: `/Users/marlin/cmux-companion/ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:123-134`
   - `connectIfPaired()` loads one `PairingCredentials` and calls `connect(to:)` once
   - `connect(to:)` (line 128) disconnects the old client, then creates **one** new `BridgeClient` instance
   - No multiplexing or bridge-switching logic

**Data model**: `PairingCredentials` (line 4-15 in PairingStore.swift) is a flat struct with `host: String`, `port: Int`, `token: String`, `tailscaleHost: String?` — designed for one server, not a collection.

## 2. One phone → multiple Macs/bridges: **No, not supported**
The iOS app is hardwired to a single bridge:
- Keychain stores **one** credential set — fixed `service`/`account`, and `save()` deletes the prior entry first (`ios/cmux/Connection/PairingStore.swift`).
- `AppState` holds a single `client: BridgeClient?` and a single `pendingPairing`, not collections (`ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:31-32`).

- `PairingCredentials` is a flat struct (`host/port/token/tailscaleHost?`) — no notion of a server list.

Here's my review of PR #14.

## PR #14 — `fix(bridge): detect cmux socket under XDG state dir and non-uid name`

**Overview:** Rewrites `DetectSocketPath` to probe both pointer-file locations (XDG state dir + Application Support) and both socket-name conventions (`cmux-<uid>.sock` and plain `cmux.sock`) before falling back to `/tmp/cmux.sock`. +45/−15, one file. Fixes a real failure (verified live on the Mac mini: the old code fell through to the non-existent `/tmp` socket).

### Correctness — solid
- The root-cause fix is right: the mini wrote its pointer under XDG and named the socket `cmux.sock`; both are now covered.
- Priority ordering is sound: a pointer whose socket **actually exists** wins first; then direct socket probes; then a non-validated pointer; then `/tmp`. A live socket correctly beats a dead pointer.
- The uid-suffixed candidate is probed before plain `cmux.sock`, so machines like the MacBook (which have *both* files present) still resolve to the same socket they did before.

### Behavior change worth calling out (improvement, but note it)
- The old code returned the Application Support pointer's **contents unconditionally** if the file was non-empty — even if that socket was stale/gone. The new code only returns a pointer early if its socket `Stat`s cleanly, otherwise it keeps probing. That's strictly better (validates liveness), but it *is* a semantic change for anyone who had a stale pointer file — they'll now get a probed real socket instead of a dead path. Worth a line in the PR body; no action needed.
- The final fallback improved from "always `/tmp/cmux.sock`" to "the first pointer's path if any pointer existed." Better diagnostics (the caller's dial error names a plausible path, not `/tmp`).

### Main gap — no test
- `DetectSocketPath` went from trivial to branchy (two loops, an existence-vs-fallback distinction) with **zero test coverage**. This is the one thing I'd push on. It's currently untestable because it reads real paths under `os.UserHomeDir()` + `os.Getuid()`.
- Suggest extracting the pure logic so it's table-testable:
  ```go
  func DetectSocketPath() string {
      home, err := os.UserHomeDir()
      if err != nil { return "/tmp/cmux.sock" }
      return detectSocketPath(home, os.Getuid())
  }
  func detectSocketPath(home string, uid int) string { ... }
  ```
  Then a temp-dir table test can cover the cases that actually regressed: XDG-pointer-only, plain `cmux.sock`, stale-pointer-falls-through-to-probe, and nothing-present → `/tmp`. Given the whole point of the PR is "detection missed a case," a test locking the matrix down is high-value.

### Minor / optional
- Nit: `os.Stat` follows symlinks, but the pointer content is written by the local trusted cmux app, so no traversal concern — fine as-is.
- The two path lists are clear and idiomatic; no perf concern (a handful of `Stat`s).
- No dedup between the pointer path and the probe candidates, but it can't double-return (first match wins), so it's harmless.

### Verdict
**Approve** with a request to add the unit test (and ideally the small refactor to enable it). Correct, well-commented, low-risk fix; the only real weakness is test coverage on logic that just proved it can silently regress.

Confirmed. The bridge's embedded Tailscale node (`cmux-bridge-mini`) has **never been logged in** — it's stuck in `NeedsLogin`, looping on `up failed` and printing the same login URL. It is **not on your tailnet**.

Here's the mechanism: `cmux-bridge --pair --tailscale` calls `startTailscaleForPairing`, which spins up the bridge's own `tsnet` node and waits (60s) for it to come up so it can read back the `.ts.net` hostname. Because that node was never authenticated, `tsnet.Up` fails, the function returns an **empty** host, and `PrintQR` then falls back to the LAN-only QR (and even prints the misleading "re-run `--pair --tailscale`" hint — which you already did).

So `--tailscale` *was* honored; it just had nothing to embed because the node isn't authenticated. That auth is the one-time interactive step I flagged earlier that hasn't been completed.

## Fix — authenticate the bridge's Tailscale node (one time)

1. On any browser signed into your tailnet (`tail901772.ts.net`, owner `moltopenclawbot@`), open the login URL the daemon is currently offering:

3. Re-run pairing — now the QR will include the tailnet host:

## Problem

Running \`cmux-bridge --pair --tailscale\` could print a **LAN-only** QR even though \`--tailscale\` was passed. The phone then paired "successfully" but sat on **reconnecting** whenever it was off the home Wi-Fi.

Root cause: if the bridge's embedded tsnet node wasn't authenticated yet, \`startTailscaleForPairing\` blocked until a 60s timeout, returned an empty host, and \`PrintQR\` silently fell back to a QR with no \`tailscale_host\`. The one hint it printed ("re-run \`--pair --tailscale\`") was misleading because the user *had* passed the flag — the real blocker was an un-authorized Tailscale node.

## Fix

- **Surface the login URL.** tsnet emits the interactive auth URL through its \`Logf\`; we now parse it out and print a clear "Tailscale login required — open this URL and approve `<hostname>`" message, then wait up to **3 minutes** for authorization (was a silent 60s).
- **Never silently degrade.** If the node still doesn't come up, \`--pair\` now **fails loudly** with actionable guidance (authorize the node; and if the background daemon is running, stop it first since it holds the tsnet state dir) instead of emitting a LAN-only QR.

Behavior when the node is already authorized is unchanged: \`ts.Up\` returns immediately and the QR includes the tailnet host.

## Testing

one orphan (old pre-tailscale binary, started before the 23:56 rebuild) held the port
while launchd crash-looped the new binary every 10s. Zero `tailscale:` lines in a 33k-line
